segments.say: Everyone who has a profile has made a series of choices. Which photo to show, which news to share, which joke to post, which day to leave out. Without quite meaning to, we become editors of our own lives, and we have an audience. Psychologists have long studied how people present themselves, and online life gives that old subject a new stage.

In 1959, the sociologist Erving Goffman published a book called The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life. He argued that social life is like theatre. We have a front stage, where we play a role for others, and a back stage, where we relax. A waiter is polite at the table and complains in the kitchen. A profile is, in these terms, a front stage that never closes.

There's nothing sinister in impression management. It's a normal, healthy part of social life. We dress for job interviews and we choose our words at weddings. The question is what happens to us when the audience is always there.

show.title: Goffman's stage
items: Front stage: where we perform for an audience
Back stage: where we drop the act
We manage impressions all the time
Online, the front stage is permanent and public

segments.say: An obvious worry is that profiles are fake: filtered, polished, idealised. If so, we'd be comparing ourselves with fictions. But researchers have tested how much of a person actually shows up in a profile, and the answer is more reassuring than you might expect.

The team studied profiles on social networks in Germany and the United States, and had strangers judge each owner's personality from the profile alone. They compared these impressions with the owners' own descriptions and with ratings from their close friends. The strangers' impressions tracked the real personality quite well, and didn't reflect the idealised self that the owners wished they were.

show.who: Back, Stopfer, Vazire, Gaddis, Schmukle, Egloff & Gosling
show.what: Facebook profiles reflect actual personality, not self-idealization

segments.say: This is a useful correction. Profiles aren't pure fiction. They carry real information about who we are, through our words, our friends and our habits. People may polish a post, but it's harder to polish the whole pattern. So the self that appears online is neither entirely false nor entirely true. It's an edited version of the real thing.

show.sub: We are more visible than we think

segments.say: There's another side to presenting yourself, and it concerns what the act does to you. Jamie Gonzales and Jeffrey Hancock at Cornell University asked a simple question. If you spend time looking at your own profile, how do you feel about yourself afterwards? They compared it with a more familiar situation: looking at yourself in a mirror.

In an experiment, students were left alone for a few minutes in a room with a mirror, with a laptop showing their own Facebook profile, or with nothing. Those who spent time with their own profile reported higher self-esteem than the others, and the effect was linked to what they'd selected for it. Looking at a carefully chosen version of themselves seemed to give a small boost.

show.what: Mirror, mirror on the Facebook wall: effects of exposure to Facebook on self-esteem

segments.say: This is a nice contrast with the comparison findings. Looking at other people's profiles can lower our self-esteem, but looking at our own can raise it. The platform doesn't have a single effect. It depends on whether the camera faces outwards or inwards, and whom we're measuring ourselves against.

That last one matters. When we publish an identity, we feel pressure to live up to it. It can be motivating, as when people share a fitness goal, and it can be limiting, when the public self no longer fits the private one.

show.title: What self-presentation can do
items: Remind us of what we value
Give us a sense of identity

segments.say: One area where presentation has been studied closely is appearance. Filters, edits and carefully chosen angles produce faces and bodies that are often hard to match. Researchers have asked whether seeing such images makes people feel worse about how they look, and the answers depend on who is looking.

A little over a hundred young women were randomly assigned to browse Facebook, or a fashion magazine site, or a neutral site, for ten minutes. Those who browsed Facebook reported a more negative mood than the others. They also reported more concerns about their face, hair and skin, but only if they tended to compare their appearance with others.

show.what: Social comparisons on social media: the impact of Facebook on young women's body image concerns and mood

segments.say: Once more, the person matters. For women who rarely compared themselves with others, a few minutes of browsing had little effect. For those who often compared, it left a mark. That suggests that the useful step may be less about avoiding images, and more about understanding the habit of comparing that makes them hurt.

It's also worth saying that images aren't all alike. Studies on body-positive content have found some benefits for mood and body image, at least in the short term, though the research is young. What we see makes a difference, and so does what we're hoping to get from it.

show.sub: Not all images are the same

segments.say: A small stage with a curtain, and a mirror at its side. A profile is a bit of both: a place to perform, and a place to see ourselves. The research suggests that neither the stage nor the mirror is bad in itself. It's the audience we imagine, and what we're hoping to hear from it.

show.cap: A small stage and a mirror

segments.say: Here are a few questions to ask about the self you present. Who are you imagining when you post? Does your profile include ordinary days as well as highlights? And does it feel like you, or like a performance for an audience? There are no right answers. But asking helps you remain the editor of your own story, rather than a character in it. People who feel that their online self matches their real one tend to feel less strain, and the match is something you can work on, one honest post at a time.

show.title: Questions for your own profile
items: Who am I picturing when I post this?
Would I be happy to say it to a friend's face?
Does my profile include real, ordinary days?
Does it feel like me, or like a performance?

segments.say: Four terms about presenting ourselves. Impression management is shaping how others see us. The front stage, in Goffman's phrase, is where we perform for an audience. Self-presentation is the picture of ourselves that we choose to show. And self-esteem is how we feel about our own worth.

show.title: Words to keep from this chapter

segments.say: Whatever your feed looks like, your back stage is where you actually live. The kitchen, the quiet evenings, the unposted moments that no one applauds. They are the main part of your life. It may help to remember that a good life is mostly lived backstage, and that it doesn't need a caption.

So what did we learn? That we manage impressions, as Goffman described. That profiles reflect real personality more than idealised selves. That looking at your own profile can lift self-esteem slightly. And that appearance effects depend on how much a person compares.

show.sub: What the performed self taught us

segments.say: Our next chapter asks the biggest question of all. Does social media bring us closer, or leave us lonelier? And what does science say about how friendships are really made?
